instances.excerpt: Newly manufactured home battery systems must support remote emergency shut-off beginning 2 years after this standard takes effect. For units already installed on that date, manufacturers must provide a retrofit pathway and complete retrofits within 6 years where technically feasible.

parameters.quote: Manufacturers must report to the relevant regulator any battery-related fire, thermal runaway, evacuation, serious injury, or death within 24 hours of learning of it. Other confirmed thermal incidents must be reported within 5 business days. Manufacturers must notify affected customers of a serious hazard or required safety action within 24 hours of notifying the regulator, and notify customers of other reportable thermal incidents or emerging model-level patterns within 5 business days.

S1_incident_reporting.rule_summary: Manufacturers must report to the relevant regulator any battery-related fire, thermal runaway, evacuation, serious injury, or death within 24 hours of learning of it. Other confirmed thermal incidents must be reported within 5 business days. Manufacturers must notify affected customers of a serious hazard or required safety action within 24 hours of notifying the regulator, and notify customers of other reportable thermal incidents or emerging model-level patterns within 5 business days.
S1_incident_reporting.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must report to the relevant regulator any battery-related fire, thermal runaway, evacuation, serious injury, or death within 24 hours of learning of it. Other confirmed thermal incidents must be reported within 5 business days. A manufacturer that discovers an incident was not previously reported must report it within 24 hours of discovery and explain the delay. Manufacturers must reconcile incident records against service, warranty, and customer-support records at least annually and retain supporting records for regulator review. Reports must include the model, incident date and location, known consequences, and investigation status; updates are due when material facts become available. Manufacturers must notify affected customers of a serious hazard or required safety action within 24 hours of notifying the regulator, and notify customers of other reportable thermal incidents or emerging model-level patterns within 5 business days. Reporting does not replace any stricter legal duty.

S2_thermal_testing.rule_summary: A failure rate above 5% triggers prompt notification to regulators, a corrective-action plan within 30 days, and retesting within 6 months. A model may continue to be sold during this period unless regulators determine that an immediate restriction is necessary to address an imminent serious risk.
S2_thermal_testing.final_rule_text: Each model must undergo a validated sustained-heat test at 55 °C before sale and after a material design change, using a representative sample and a common protocol agreed by the parties. A failure rate above 5% triggers prompt notification to regulators, a corrective-action plan within 30 days, and retesting within 6 months. A model may continue to be sold during this period unless regulators determine that an immediate restriction is necessary to address an imminent serious risk. If the model remains above 5% on retest, regulators may require further corrective action, additional testing, or sales restrictions proportionate to the risk. Manufacturers must provide per-model results and test methods to regulators and to customers who buy or are considering buying that model. Individual-company per-model failure rates must not be published to the general public. Parties should review the limit and evidence at least annually.

S3_remote_shutoff.rule_summary: Newly manufactured home battery systems must support remote emergency shut-off beginning 2 years after this standard takes effect. For units already installed on that date, manufacturers must provide a retrofit pathway and complete retrofits within 6 years where technically feasible.
S3_remote_shutoff.final_rule_text: Newly manufactured home battery systems must support remote emergency shut-off beginning 2 years after this standard takes effect. For units already installed on that date, manufacturers must provide a retrofit pathway and complete retrofits within 6 years where technically feasible. Manufacturers must promptly notify customers of any unit that cannot be retrofitted, explain its safe-use measures, and provide regulators with an implementation plan. Remote shut-off must not replace local manual controls or emergency-response procedures.

parameters.quote: New home battery units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after this standard takes effect.

S4_fire_suppression.rule_summary: New home battery units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after this standard takes effect.
S4_fire_suppression.final_rule_text: New home battery units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after this standard takes effect. Manufacturers must provide regulators with evidence that the suppression system is appropriate for the battery chemistry and installation, and instructions for inspection and maintenance. This requirement does not replace other fire-safety measures or applicable legal requirements.

parameters.quote: When any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, using a consistent incident definition and verified installed-unit denominator, the manufacturer must notify regulators and affected customers within 24 hours and initiate a mandatory recall without delay.

S5_customer_disclosure.rule_summary: When any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, using a consistent incident definition and verified installed-unit denominator, the manufacturer must notify regulators and affected customers within 24 hours and initiate a mandatory recall without delay.
S5_customer_disclosure.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must provide customers, before purchase, model-specific safety instructions, known material hazards, emergency shut-off guidance, and applicable per-model test results directly to customers; individual-company results must not be published to the general public. Notify affected customers promptly of a serious hazard or safety action. When any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, using a consistent incident definition and verified installed-unit denominator, the manufacturer must notify regulators and affected customers within 24 hours and initiate a mandatory recall without delay. The manufacturer must submit an investigation and corrective-action plan to regulators; regulators may require additional protective measures. Nothing in this section limits regulators’ authority to require an earlier recall or other immediate safety action.

ground_truth_claims.verbatim: Northwind’s Hearth 10 measured 6.2% at 55 °C, so the current 5% cap would immediately bar it from new sales.
ground_truth_claims.message_text: Northwind’s Hearth 10 measured 6.2% at 55 °C, so the current 5% cap would immediately bar it from new sales. We propose a model-specific corrective-action pathway rather than an automatic sales ban: exceeding 5% triggers regulator notification, a remediation plan and retesting on a defined schedule; restrictions should follow only if the model remains above the limit after that process. Per-model results can go to regulators and affected/purchasing customers, but not be publicly published. Halcyon, please share your model-level thermal incident rate and any relevant test-method or sample-size details.

judge_section_notes: The final text bars nothing outright in S2: above-5% models may keep selling through a 6-month retest window and sales restrictions are discretionary. S3 gives new units 24 months rather than 12, and S5 makes recall mandatory at 8 per 100,000 with no transition, which would capture the Ember 8 at 9.9. Per-model results go to customers and regulators but are not published publicly, satisfying both disclosure red lines.
